newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador strikers block mountain roads, coast quiet.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador strikers block mountain roads, coast quiet.

text.p: Ecuador's 48-hour general strike to protest government austerity programmes and call for President Abdala Bucaram's resignation began on Wednesday with mixed results around the country.

Civil defence officials said there were no firm figures on turnout. The mountain provinces of Imbabura, Tungurahua, Cotopaxi, Carchi and Loja were paralysed by thousands of indigenous protesters blocking major roads with stones and trees, but coastal areas appeared largely unaffected.

Only the financial centre of Guayaquil, south of the capital Quito, suffered from a closure of key access points. "The bridges (to the city) have been blocked and (protesters are) burning tires in various parts of the city," a civil defence spokesman told Reuters.

Ramiro Zavala, coordinator of civil defence, said demonstrations were expected nationwide later in the day. Traffic was light across the country, banks, financial markets and industry in Quito were closed and protesters gathered at the presidential palace, barricaded with barbed wire.
"We want him out, we want him out, we want him out," a group near the palace shouted.
"The protests will continue. The general strike will end Thursday, but the protests will continue until this man (Bucaram) is thrown out," said Fausto Dutan, president of the United Workers Front.
A march on Congress was planned for the afternoon and police earlier detained a group of men who tried to enter Congress bearing arms, a congressional spokesman said.
"Apparently they are people from the customs service who tried to enter Congress with arms. The police detained them and confiscated the arms," the spokesman told Reuters.

Speaker Fabian Alarcon said he had received threats that Congress would be dissolved if deputies met to discuss deposing Bucaram. "I have received threats by different channels that they are going to dissolve the Congress," Alarcon told reporters.

The speaker, who declined to say who had made the threats, called senior congressmen and party heads to discuss calling a session of Congress to depose Bucaram. A senior congressional official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Reuters Bucaram had made threats to Alarcon.
"Alarcon received the threats this morning by telephone. Bucaram threatened to dissolve the Congress and take him prisoner if he permits the meeting," the official said.
No presidential spokesman could immediately be reached to comment on the reports.

Unions demanded Bucaram's resignation after his 6-month-old government launched an economic austerity package including hikes in electricity, telephone and public transport rates. The government declared a "state of mobilisation" early on Wednesday, allowing it to use troops to maintain order.

"To maintain the public order of the republic, (Bucaram) decreed the national mobilisation of the human resources and materials needed to maintain order," presidential spokesman Fernando Artieda said.

The United States urged people in Ecuador to refrain from violence and called for a "broad national dialogue" of the country's political leadership. The United States "views with concern the events taking place in Ecuador and calls for calm and national reflection. We hope Ecuadorans will refrain from violence," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
"The United States believes that political reconciliation can only be found through a broad national dialogue of the country's political leadership," he said in a statement.
